library(metrodag)
```

## One graph can support several analysis views

A DAG describes assumed causal relationships. The exposure, outcome, and
adjustment set describe a particular analysis of that graph. Keeping those
decisions separate helps a reader see exactly what changes between analyses.

This guide uses the smoking example from [Getting started](metrodag.html).
It is self-contained: run the code below even if you have not worked through
that guide. The example is a teaching model, not an empirically established DAG.

```{r graph}
edges <- data.frame(
  from = c("C", "C", "X", "X", "M"),
  to   = c("X", "Y", "M", "Y", "Y")
)
display_labels <- c(C = "Socioeconomic background", X = "Cigarettes per day",
  M = "Tar deposits", Y = "Lung cancer")
g <- igraph::graph_from_data_frame(edges, directed = TRUE)
fixed <- layout_metro_dag(g, direction = "right")
```

`layout_metro_dag()` computes geometry once. Pass that layout to subsequent
plots to retain every variable, arrow, and route. When reusing it, omit layout
arguments such as `direction`, `rank`, and `align`; those decisions have already
been made.

## Read the variable markers

| Annotation | Appearance | Meaning in the displayed analysis |
|:--|:--|:--|
| `exposure = "X"` | Filled exposure marker | The chosen exposure |
| `outcome = "Y"` | Filled outcome marker | The chosen outcome |
| `adjusted = "C"` | Filled square | A variable chosen for adjustment |
| `unobserved = "U"` | Dashed circle and outgoing arrows | A variable treated as unobserved |
| `selected = "P"` | Double-outlined square | A variable conditioned on by selection, such as hospital admission |
| No explicit role | Hollow circle | An observed variable without another role |

These five explicit roles must be disjoint: for example, an unobserved variable
cannot also be marked as adjusted, and a selected variable cannot also be an
adjustment covariate. Observed does not mean adjusted, and
unadjusted does not mean unobserved. A variable can also have an independent
display category, introduced below.

The package does not infer that a variable is a confounder, mediator, or collider
from its name. Such descriptions depend on the graph and the question. The
graphical basis for choosing adjustment sets is discussed by
[Textor et al. (2016)](https://doi.org/10.1093/ije/dyw341).

## Compare an unadjusted and an adjusted analysis

```{r views}
crude <- metro_dag(fixed, labels = display_labels,
  exposure = "X", outcome = "Y", unadjusted = TRUE,
  estimand = "Unadjusted X-Y association")

adjusted <- metro_dag(fixed, labels = display_labels,
  exposure = "X", outcome = "Y", adjusted = "C",
  estimand = "Total effect of X on Y")
```

`unadjusted = TRUE` explicitly selects no adjustment variables. In contrast,
omitting adjustment arguments leaves the set unspecified unless it is inherited
from the input. An explicit empty set is useful for comparisons and causal
checks; it prevents a reader from confusing "no adjustment" with "not reported".

Use `compare_metro_dags()` to present both analyses at the same physical scale
with one shared legend:

```{r comparison, fig.height=3.8, fig.cap="The assumed graph remains fixed while the adjustment annotations change.", fig.alt="Two panels show identical nodes and arrows. The unadjusted panel has no adjusted variables; the total-effect panel marks socioeconomic background as adjusted."}
comparison_labels <- display_labels
comparison_labels["C"] <- "Socioeconomic\nbackground"
comparison <- compare_metro_dags(fixed, labels = comparison_labels,
  label_wrap = NULL, views = list(
  Unadjusted = list(exposure = "X", outcome = "Y", unadjusted = TRUE,
    estimand = "Unadjusted X-Y association"),
  Adjusted = list(exposure = "X", outcome = "Y", adjusted = "C",
    estimand = "Total effect of X on Y")
))
comparison
```

In this assumed graph, `C` blocks the back-door path from `X` to `Y`. Leaving
`M` out of the adjustment set retains the pathway through tar deposits in the
total-effect target. These interpretations depend on the assumed graph.

`estimand` supplies a descriptive title. It does not estimate an effect or
establish identification. Different adjustment sets can target the same effect,
and adding a mediator to the controls does not by itself establish a direct
effect. Use a suitable causal analysis for that question.

Set `ncol = 1` to stack panels when each needs more horizontal space.
`comparison$plots` contains the individual plots, and `comparison$layout`
contains their shared geometry.

## Check adjustment separately

The optional dagitty package provides graphical adjustment criteria. Metrodag's
`check_metro_adjustment()` delegates a **total-effect** check to DAGitty; plotting
never runs it automatically. Install the dependency once if needed:

```{r install-dagitty, eval=FALSE}
install.packages("dagitty")
```

```{r adjustment-check}
if (requireNamespace("dagitty", quietly = TRUE)) {
  print(check_metro_adjustment(crude))
  print(check_metro_adjustment(adjusted))
}
```

For this graph, the empty set fails the criterion and adjusting for `C` passes.
The returned object's `valid` field records the result. A passing result concerns
graphical identification by adjustment under the specified DAG; it does not
validate the graph, measurements, positivity, or statistical estimator, and does
not check direct or indirect effects. See
[Textor et al. (2016)](https://doi.org/10.1093/ije/dyw341) for the DAGitty methods.

## Reuse annotations deliberately

A plot stores its annotated layout in `attr(p, "metrodag_layout")`. Reusing
that layout inherits its roles. A supplied vector replaces the old
set rather than adding to it:

```{r inheritance}
annotated_layout <- attr(adjusted, "metrodag_layout")
cleared <- metro_dag(annotated_layout, labels = display_labels,
  unadjusted = TRUE, estimand = "Unadjusted X-Y association")
attr(cleared, "metrodag_analysis")$adjusted
```

| Intention | Argument |
|:--|:--|
| Inherit an existing role | Omit the role or supply `NULL` |
| Replace an adjustment set | `adjusted = c("C", "Z")`, when both nodes exist |
| Clear a role | For example, `unobserved = character(0)` or `selected = character(0)` |
| Explicitly select no adjustment | `unadjusted = TRUE` or `adjusted = character(0)` |
| Clear an inherited target title | `estimand = NULL` |

An omitted estimand title is inherited only when exposure and outcome stay the
same. If you change either target, the omitted title is cleared. Supply a new
title when the analysis question changes.

## Show unobserved variables and custom categories

Suppose we expand the teaching graph to include two unmeasured influences.
`U1` affects smoking and lung cancer; `U2` affects tar deposits and lung cancer.
Neither can be marked as adjusted. The example illustrates how to display these
assumptions, not how to recover a causal effect in their presence.

```{r groups, fig.height=5.5, fig.cap="Dashed markers describe observability; numbered categories add an independent description.", fig.alt="A six-node graph with dashed U1 and U2 nodes. Numbered groups distinguish exposure factors from mediator factors, while X and Y retain their exposure and outcome markers."}
expanded_edges <- rbind(edges, data.frame(
  from = c("U1", "U1", "U2", "U2"),
  to = c("X", "Y", "M", "Y")
))
grouped <- metro_dag(expanded_edges,
  labels = c(display_labels, U1 = "Smoking-related genes",
    U2 = "Airway clearance genes"),
  exposure = "X", outcome = "Y", unobserved = c("U1", "U2"),
  node_groups = list(
    "Exposure factors" = c("X", "U1"),
    "Mediator factors" = c("M", "U2")
  ),
  node_group_colours = c("Exposure factors" = "#006D5B",
    "Mediator factors" = "#7A5195"),
  style = "monochrome")
grouped
```

Each node can belong to one display group alongside its analysis role. Numbered
marks and matching legend entries identify the groups in every style; numbers
follow category names in UTF-8 byte order. Optional outline colours appear in
publication or metro style. Monochrome retains the numbers but ignores those
colours. Groups do not change node positions, routes, or the causal checks.

Use `node_groups = list()` to clear inherited categories. To clear only colour
overrides, use `node_group_colours = character(0)`. For a comparison, pass groups
to `compare_metro_dags()` itself so every panel shares one category mapping.

A group named "Selection factors" is only a display category. It does not
encode conditioning on hospital admission. Use the `selected` role, described
next, when the analysis is restricted to selected patients.

## Show selection and highlight open paths

Restricting an analysis to hospitalised patients conditions on admission.
Mark such variables with `selected`: they are drawn as squares with a double
outline and listed as "Selected (conditioned on)" in the legend. Selection is
not an adjustment choice, and `check_metro_adjustment()` refuses graphs with
selected variables rather than silently ignoring them.

`highlight_paths()` asks DAGitty for the paths between exposure and outcome
and emphasises the arrows on paths that remain open given the adjustment set
and any selected variables. It changes only arrow appearance; the layout and
roles are unchanged, and `attr(p, "metrodag_paths")` lists every path with its
status.

```{r selection-graph}
sel_edges <- data.frame(
  from = c("C", "C", "X", "M", "X", "X", "Y"),
  to   = c("X", "Y", "M", "Y", "Y", "P", "P"))
sel_labels <- c(C = "Socioeconomic background", X = "Cigarettes per day",
  M = "Tar deposits", Y = "Lung cancer", P = "Hospital admission")
```

```{r selection-paths, fig.height=3.6, fig.cap="Conditioning on hospital admission opens a path through it; adjustment for C closes the confounding path.", fig.alt="A DAG with exposure X, outcome Y, adjusted C and selected admission P. Arrows on the open paths X to M to Y, X to Y and X to P from Y are drawn thicker in red; the paths through C are grey."}
if (requireNamespace("dagitty", quietly = TRUE)) {
  selected_plot <- metro_dag(sel_edges, labels = sel_labels, exposure = "X",
    outcome = "Y", adjusted = "C", selected = "P")
  highlighted <- highlight_paths(selected_plot)
  print(highlighted)
  attr(highlighted, "metrodag_paths")[, c("path", "open")]
}
```

Use `paths = "biasing"` to emphasise only the open non-causal paths that an
adjustment set should close (with several exposures, paths through another
exposure are left out, as in DAGitty's adjustment criterion), `paths = "causal"` for open directed paths, or
`paths = "all"` for every path; the `causal` column of the path table says
which is which. Describe the colour convention in the figure caption.

## Mark assumptions about individual arrows

`edge_style` changes the linetype, colour or width of named arrows, and
`edge_legend` explains a linetype in the legend. A dotted arrow is a common way
to show a relationship that is assumed but uncertain:

```{r edge-legend, fig.height=3.4, fig.cap="A dotted arrow marks an uncertain assumption, explained in the legend.", fig.alt="The smoking DAG with a dotted arrow from socioeconomic background to lung cancer and a legend entry reading Assumed, uncertain."}
metro_dag(sel_edges[1:5, ], labels = sel_labels[c("C", "X", "M", "Y")], exposure = "X", outcome = "Y",
  adjusted = "C", edge_style = list("C->Y" = list(linetype = "dotted")),
  edge_legend = c(dotted = "Assumed, uncertain"))
```

## Starting from DAGitty

Directed DAGitty DAGs can be passed directly to `metro_dag()`. Node identifiers,
isolated nodes, and exposure, outcome, adjusted, and latent statuses are retained.
Positions are recomputed by metrodag.

```{r dagitty-import, fig.cap="A directed DAGitty graph imported with its analysis roles.", fig.alt="DAGitty's X exposure, Y outcome, C adjustment marker, and latent U are retained in the metrodag drawing."}
if (requireNamespace("dagitty", quietly = TRUE)) {
  dag <- dagitty::dagitty("dag {
    X [exposure]; Y [outcome]; C [adjusted]; U [latent]
    C -> X; C -> Y; X -> M; M -> Y; X -> Y; U -> C
  }")
  metro_dag(dag)
}
```

The imported roles must be disjoint. DAGitty `[selected]` nodes are imported
with the `selected` role. Undirected and partially directed edges are
unsupported.

A bidirected arc `A <-> B` states that A and B share an unobserved common
cause. By default such graphs are rejected so the assumption is never dropped
silently. With `bidirected = "latent"`, each arc is drawn as an unlabelled,
dashed unobserved variable with arrows into both endpoints. That expanded DAG
encodes the same assumption for adjustment checks:

```{r dagitty-bidirected, fig.height=3, fig.cap="A bidirected arc drawn as an unlabelled unobserved common cause.", fig.alt="X and Y joined by a direct arrow and by dashed arrows from an unlabelled dashed station, with C adjusted."}
if (requireNamespace("dagitty", quietly = TRUE)) {
  confounded <- dagitty::dagitty("dag {
    X [exposure]; Y [outcome]; C [adjusted]
    C -> X; C -> Y; X -> Y; X <-> Y
  }")
  metro_dag(confounded, bidirected = "latent")
}
```
